🐾 Here’s the story behind Matt’s payments work at **JP Morgan Chase**.

From **August 2009 to June 2012**, Matt served as Technology Delivery Lead for ACCESS Next Generation, the bank’s unified corporate banking portal. The challenge went beyond installing Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform: the bank needed purpose-built payment capabilities, while its regional systems had different data models, permissions, payment formats, and regulatory requirements. Legacy entitlement changes took days of manual configuration, and live payments had to continue throughout migration.

Matt managed a blended team of **40+** **Accenture** and bank resources across Mumbai, Bangalore, and the US. He spent **70 to 80%** of his time embedded at Bottomline’s Portsmouth offices, working through where WebSeries’ native capabilities ended and custom engineering was required.

He designed and delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and federal tax payment modules, including NACHA file validation, payment-integrity verification through Message Authentication Codes, and payment-type-specific permissions. He also designed the centralized gateway for message transformation, protocol translation, and routing across **12 countries**, connecting ACCESS to clearing networks and internal compliance, settlement, and reporting systems.

For corporate administrators, Matt replaced individual permission configuration with role-based profiles, bulk changes, and a centralized dashboard. Entitlement management dropped from **days to minutes**. He also led payments data migration and coordinated jurisdiction-specific access and data-visibility controls with regional compliance teams, sequencing launches by regulatory readiness rather than a single global deployment.

ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, serving **135,000+** corporations, financial institutions, governments, and municipalities across **180+ countries**. The gateway replaced fragmented regional integrations with a single payment entry point. Migration completed with **zero disruption to live payment operations**, and the regional compliance framework enabled launches across APAC, EMEA, and the Americas without regulatory blockers.

🐾 Here’s how Matt describes his leadership philosophy.

Matt leads with empathy, clarity, and purpose. His goal is to create an environment where engineers, designers, and product teams can do the best work of their careers. Many teams he inherited were “over-processed, under-trusted, waiting for permission instead of owning outcomes.” He focused on removing those barriers rather than adding more process.

He makes intent explicit, pushes decisions to the people closest to the work, and uses transparency, direct feedback, and open communication. He coaches teams to think clearly, not just execute tasks. His non-negotiables include psychological safety, integrity and respect, continuous learning, and “outcomes, not optics.”

At the **Accenture** Cloud Innovation Center, that included a “permit to fail” culture. Teams had avoided risks because they feared blame. Matt organized non-punitive post-mortems and supported lean, low-stakes experiments with structured hypotheses and controlled iterations. Team members began experimenting more freely, applying lessons to subsequent sprints, and preventing repeat failure patterns. In product incubation, he set expectations that early prototypes and user tests would likely fail: the goal was to reduce risk quickly and cheaply, not be right on the first try.

He also assembled balanced teams of engineers, product managers, and UX architects with equal participation and shared accountability. Pair programming, collaborative coding, and retrospectives replaced siloed work and excessive handoffs. Teams could voice feedback and implement changes autonomously.

At the Cloud Innovation Center, teams accelerated delivery **4x** after embracing lean product and modern engineering practices. The balanced-team work also reduced project delays, improved retention, and achieved **zero-defect production code**.

answer_md:
🐾 Matt builds products, platforms, and the teams that deliver them.

His work spans Execution & Delivery, Org & Working-Model Transformation, and Talent & Enablement. He came up from software engineer to Director, delivering enterprise platforms before building **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Centers in Atlanta and Tampa.

The centers addressed a specific problem: clients wanted to move beyond waterfall delivery, feature factories, and siloed teams, but startup practices needed adapting for legacy systems, compliance, and enterprise governance. New hires also needed hands-on experience with cloud-native technologies and modern engineering practices.

Matt brought product managers, designers, and engineers into balanced teams. He combined customer interviews, hypothesis-driven design, and thin-slice, production-ready delivery with pair programming, test-driven development, and automated pipelines. Training followed an “I do, we do, you do” progression, with mentoring, coding katas, and practice learning sessions rather than concept-only instruction.

When those practices failed to take hold at **Norfolk Southern**, Matt did not defend the dashboard. The client was finding defects despite near-complete test coverage. He took ownership, audited the code and tests, and found tests written after the code alongside vague backlog stories. He rebuilt the backlog with testable stories and brought in experts to work beside the engineers. The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see.

Across the CIC practice, Matt grew the organization from **0 to 150+ practitioners**, with full P&L accountability. The centers delivered **30+ product engagements** across **15+ Fortune 500 clients**, achieving **4X faster velocity** and zero-defect deployments through TDD and automated pipelines. At **JP Morgan**, teams outpaced peer velocity within the first **2 sprints**. Delivery excellence and returning clients contributed to **\$100M+ in repeatable business by FY23**.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s a time Matt’s assumptions led to a production-data incident.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization for a financial services client. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams running test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production environments. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with existing documentation.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup. Instead of verifying those controls, he assumed they were correct and focused on delivery pressures. He did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, confirm that production customer names and email addresses had been scrubbed, or implement compensating controls such as data masking and email interception.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**. The root cause was insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed from downstream environments.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. He worked collectively with the team to understand what happened and implement corrective controls. But the consequences included someone’s place on the team: the client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described it as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.”

Afterward, Matt made IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach. His stated lesson was that “assumptions are risks in disguise,” and that leaders own the environment their teams operate in.

He did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, confirm that production customer names and email addresses had been scrubbed, or implement compensating controls such as data masking and email interception.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**. The root cause was insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed from downstream environments.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. He worked collectively with the team to understand what happened and implement corrective controls. But the consequences included someone’s place on the team: the client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described it as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.”

Afterward, Matt made IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach. His stated lesson was that “assumptions are risks in disguise,” and that leaders own the environment their teams operate in.

answer_md:
🐾 Found it!

At **Accenture’s** Liquid Studio, traditional training programs couldn’t keep pace with rapidly evolving AWS technologies. Engineers had gaps in cloud competency, and cloud adoption was slowing. The AWS Launchpad program was designed to give engineers structured cloud training and practical experience, rather than relying on theory alone.

Matt led Launchpad at the Atlanta Innovation Hub from **July 2018** to **November 2019**, working in collaboration with AWS. He designed structured learning paths and certification programs around AWS core services and cloud-native application development. The curriculum included Lambda, API Gateway, DynamoDB, Kubernetes, and ECS/Fargate.

The program combined those learning paths with interactive workshops and hands-on labs. Engineers worked in real-world AWS environments to reinforce practical application over theory. Certification preparation sat alongside that practical work, with support for AWS Solutions Architect and DevOps Engineer certifications.

Matt also established cloud expert mentorship teams so engineers had people to learn from as they developed their cloud competencies. He organized group coaching sessions and knowledge-sharing workshops, giving participants opportunities to work through questions together and share what they were learning. The mentorship teams embedded AWS best practices and institutional knowledge beyond the individual training sessions.

More than **200 professionals earned AWS certifications** through the program. Engineers gained practical cloud experience alongside their credentials, and the program accelerated cloud adoption and the launch of cloud-native initiatives at **Accenture**. The learning paths, labs, mentoring, and group coaching supported ongoing capability-building across teams.
